item.title: Maya mathematician’s name decoded alongside astronomical formula
item.description: Hieroglyphs on the wall of a Maya building record calculations concerning the orbits of Earth, Mars and Venus, as well as the name of a mathematician who wrote the text around 1200 years ago

item.title: We finally know the name of a Maya mathematician
item.description: The signature of Sak Tahn Waax, or “White-Chested Fox,” was found inscribed in a 1,000-year-old chamber beneath present-day Guatemala

item.title: Scientists Did the Math on Cannibalism. Apparently Eating Other People Is Not Good for Your Health
item.description: New study suggests prion disease, not calories, made cannibalism an evolutionary dead end.

item.title: How humans evolved to be twice as big as our ancestors
item.description: Artistic representations of ancient humans often show large men with bulging muscles – but our ancestors were actually smaller than us, in both height and body mass. Columnist Michael Marshall reveals surprising details about the short kings of prehistory

item.title: The Brain Has Its Own Drainage System and It May Work Differently in Chronic Fatigue Syndrome

item.title: Sugar molecules found in interstellar space for the first time
item.description: Researchers have long suspected early life may have been helped by sugars brought to Earth by asteroids – now a sugar found in raspberries has been spotted in a cosmic cloud nearly 27 light years away

item.title: Alzheimer’s, stroke, depression: The preventative power of sauna
item.description: Sustained heat stress is bad for our health and can be deadly. But we’re discovering that heat therapies like sauna, when used in the right way, have surprisingly wide-reaching benefits for health

item.title: Scientists spot sugar in interstellar space for the first time ever
item.description: Erythrulose—a sugar found in raspberries—is also prevalent in a giant molecular cloud close to our galaxy’s core, scientists have discovered

item.title: Why climate scientists need to talk more about the very worst-case scenarios
item.description: London probably won’t disappear beneath the waves. But we still need to understand the most dangerous outcomes that remain possible – and avoidable.

item.title: Tiny Underwater Waves in the Ocean Can Affect the Climate Thousands of Kilometres Away
item.description: Thousands of metres below the ocean’s surface, there are tiny waves moving through the water. Much like breaking waves at the beach, these small waves within the ocean must eventually break. When they do, they create turbulence and mixing, similar to what you feel from a big wave breaking on the beach. This might seem […]
